blocks.text: When two bodies travelling along an axis do not end up traveling along the same initial axis after collision, then it is a case of two-dimensional collision. When the collision is elastic, the system of bodies conserves both its total linear momentum and total kinetic energy.

Consider two bodies colliding elastically at a certain glancing angle, showing that the collision is not head-on. Let m₁ be the mass of the first body (projectile) moving with initial velocity v⃗₁i and m₂ is the mass of the body second (target), which is initially at rest, v⃗₂i = 0. As the two bodies collide together, the impulses generated between them, send these bodies off at angles θ₁ and θ₂ to the x-axis, along which the projectile initially travelled.

blocks.alt: x and y axes with ball m₂ at rest at the origin. Ball m₁ comes from the left with velocity v₁ᵢ along the x-axis. After the collision m₂ moves off above the x-axis at angle θ₂ with velocity v₂f, and m₁ moves off below the x-axis at angle θ₁ with velocity v₁f.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.15: Elastic collision in two dimensions (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.15).

blocks.text: An elastic collision that is not a head-on collision between two bodies.
Initially, the body with mass m₂ (target), is at rest.

The initial momentum of projectile before collision is m₁v⃗₁i while initial momentum of target before collision is zero. The final momentum of projectile having mass m₁ and velocity v⃗₁f after collision is m₁v⃗₁f. The final momentum of target having mass m₂ and velocity v⃗₂f after collision is m₂v⃗₂f. Resolve final momentum of projectile into components m₁v⃗₁f cosθ₁ and m₁v⃗₁f sinθ₁. Similarly, resolve the final momentum of target into components m₂v⃗₂f cosθ₂ and m₂v⃗₂f sinθ₂.

blocks.text_alt: Momentum before collision = Momentum after collision
m₁v₁i = m₁v₁f cos θ₁ + m₂v₂f cos θ₂
m₁v₁i - m₁v₁f cos θ₁ = m₂v₂f cos θ₂   (2.34)
Momentum before collision = Momentum after collision
0 = m₁v₁f sin θ₁ - m₂v₂f sin θ₂
m₁v₁f sin θ₁ = m₂v₂f sin θ₂   (2.35)

blocks.text: Analysis of the above equation reveals that there are four unknown quantities, v⃗₁f, v⃗₂f, θ₁, θ₂. If these quantities can be measured, conservation of momentum and energy can be proved using equation (2.34), (2.35) and (2.36).

blocks.title: Interesting Information
blocks.text: Some of the kinetic energy is transferred into other forms such as heat, sound, and deformation in inelastic collision. For example, the collision is inelastic if a bullet is fired into a block of wood. This is because some energy of the bullet is lost in the form of sound and heat. Similarly, if a ball is dropped on a floor from a certain height, it does not rebound to the same height because its kinetic energy is lost in other forms of energies, like sound energy and heat energy.

blocks.title: Example 2.9
blocks.problem: A particle 'A' of mass 1 kg is moving with initial velocity 5 m s⁻¹ towards right collides with stationary target 'B' of same mass at rest. After collision the particle 'A' moves at an angle of 30° above horizontal with a speed of 3 m s⁻¹ and particle 'B' moves with the horizontal at an angle of 53° with a speed of 4 m s⁻¹. Prove that collision is elastic in nature.
steps:
Initial momentum = m₁v₁i + m₂v₂i
= (1 kg × 5 m s⁻¹) + (1 kg × 0 m s⁻¹) = 5 kg m s⁻¹

Final momentum in x-direction = m₁v₁f + m₂v₂f
= (1 kg × 3 m s⁻¹ × cos30°) + (1 kg × 4 m s⁻¹ × cos53°)
= 2.60 kg m s⁻¹ + 2.40 kg m s⁻¹
= 5 kg m s⁻¹

As momentum is conserved in x-direction, therefore,
(K.E)i = ½m₁v₁i² + ½m₂v₂i²
= (½ × 1 × (5)²) + (½ × 1 × 0) = 12.5 J
blocks.answer: As both momentum and K.E. are conserved, indicating that collision is elastic.
